A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EEmoDB and EEmo-Logic. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across inserted sections and pagination changes.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, training ablations and human validation of generated VAD labels in Section 5 and Appendices C and F.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and reports additional human validation, controlled comparisons, robustness tests and reward ablations.

M1.justification: The proposed Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone, LoRA SFT followed by GRPO, and ranking, hybrid-regression and emotion-similarity rewards remain unchanged. V2 evaluates alternatives through ablations without replacing the proposed method.

E1.justification: The seven source datasets and evaluation coverage remain unchanged: EEmo-Bench, Artphoto, ArtEmis, UNIAA Sentiment and AesBench AesE. Additional audits and controls use retained data and tasks; semantically equivalent prompts preserve task requirements.

E2.justification: V2 additionally evaluates Emotion-Qwen after SFT on EEmoDB against EEmo-Logic in Table 14. This introduces an adapted comparator trained on the proposed dataset, while the original comparator sets in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix C.2 revises discrete VAD validation from 180 samples and three experts to 1,800 samples and five experts. V2 adds continuous validation using 600 samples, six annotators and a nine-point SAM scale, plus a 400-instance QA evaluation by three annotators. New experiments also introduce shared-data fine-tuning controls, paraphrased prompts and textual/semantic reasoning-consistency checks.

E4.justification: Beyond v1’s stage/task ablations, v2 tests full fine-tuning followed by GRPO, expands annotation-quality validation, and adds reasoning–answer consistency and prompt-variation analyses. Tables 15–17 newly ablate format-reward weight, the squared ranking margin, regression reward and emotion-similarity reward parameters.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 first reports Krippendorff’s alpha for discrete and continuous VAD annotations, adding inter-annotator reliability estimation to v1’s agreement reporting. The existing repeated cross-validation and five-round LLM judging remain unchanged; model-seed variability and confidence intervals are not newly reported.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their results, but v2 adds substantial validation, training-loss, consistency, prompt-control, baseline and reward-ablation results. Appendix C.2 replaces VAD agreement rates of 83.33%, 83.33% and 80% with 94.00%, 93.83% and 91.17% under the enlarged study, so these are not matched-protocol gains. Table 4 changes the final model’s Artphoto F1 from 40.31% to 38.68%, matching the retained Table 3 value.

T1.justification: Equations 1–13, the CES-to-VAD mapping assumptions, training objectives and reward definitions are retained. The added explanations and empirical reward comparisons introduce no new formal results, derivations or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: the large unified EEmoDB dataset, a two-stage emotion-assessment framework, and strong in-domain and cross-domain performance. New experiments support these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation of dataset reliability and training effectiveness. It distinguishes discrete and continuous validation roles, discusses ambiguity from plausible distractors, and adds explanations involving catastrophic forgetting, emergent reasoning consistency, prompt robustness and reward weighting. Appendix F.5 newly discusses training-data confounding and attributes the controlled comparison’s advantage to the multi-stage framework.

D1.justification: Table 10 newly discloses comparative SFT settings, including full fine-tuning’s learning rate, global batch size, weight decay and warmup ratio; this does not establish changes to existing experiments. The abstract replaces the anonymous code link with GitHub access described as covering both dataset and code, and the Ethics Statement specifies CC BY-NC 4.0 licensing.

R1.justification: V2 replaces the Ekman 1982 chapter with the distinct 1992 article, An argument for basic emotions, and briefly connects reasoning consistency to DeepSeek-R1 in Appendix F.4. The broader related-work positioning remains stable; other bibliographic updates concern retained works.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized wording and formatting edits, adds equal-contribution and conference information, acknowledgements and an Ethics Statement, and expands several appendix subsections. The main narrative and section order remain largely intact; retained prompt sections are principally renumbered.

P2.justification: V2 adds a substantial appendix table suite, Tables 10–17, displaying settings, training losses, consistency checks, prompt sensitivity, the adapted baseline and reward ablations. Table 4 gains another experimental row. Existing Figures 1–13 are retained, with caption and placement adjustments rather than replacement.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses central evidential gaps in v1: expanded human validation tests continuous synthetic scores and generated QA, while the shared-data baseline and reward ablations strengthen support for the framework’s contribution beyond aggregate benchmark performance. These additions substantially improve rigor. Some interpretations remain overstated: reasoning–answer consistency does not establish reasoning correctness, and one adapted baseline does not fully isolate architectural effects.
